cards.front: What does the Python shell do with what you type?
cards.back: Evaluates it

cards.text: Every expression evaluates to {{c1::a value}}; every value is {{c2::an object}}; every object has {{c3::a type}}
cards.extra: The chain the whole language rests on.

cards.front: How do you find out an object's type?
cards.back: type(4) — it returns the class

cards.front: What is the relationship between “class” and “type” in Python?
cards.back: Basically interchangeable

cards.front: How many integer types does Python have, and what do they cover?
cards.back: One — it stores both small and large values. Floats are the same way

cards.front: Are Python floats exact?
cards.back: No — they are not 100% precise

cards.front: What is a float structurally analogous to?
cards.back: Scientific notation — a mantissa and an exponent, in binary

cards.front: Why are floats imprecise?
cards.back: The mantissa and exponent each have only a limited number of digits available

cards.front:
What does this print?
print(0.1 + 0.2)
cards.back: 0.30000000000000004 — the limited mantissa cannot represent 0.1 or 0.2 exactly

cards.front: What type does / return, whatever its operands?
cards.back: A float

cards.front: What does // do, and what type does it return?
cards.back: Floor division — drops the fractional portion and returns an int

cards.front:
What does this print?
print(7 / 2)
cards.back: 3.5

cards.front:
What does this print?
print(7 // 2)
cards.back: 3

cards.front:
What does this print?
print(-7 // 2)
cards.back: -4, not -3 — // floors toward negative infinity rather than truncating. See the draft note.

cards.front: What is % useful for?
cards.back: Repeating patterns

cards.front: How do you get the last digit of a number?
cards.back: Mod it by 10

cards.front: How do you test whether a number is even or odd?
cards.back: Mod it by 2 — the result is 0 or 1

cards.front:
What does this print?
print(17 % 10)
cards.back: 7

cards.meaning: which operator Python evaluates first when they differ in level
which operand goes first when operators are at the same level

cards.front: Which way do addition and subtraction associate?
cards.back: To the left — the leftmost goes first

cards.front: Which way does exponentiation associate?
cards.back: To the right

cards.text: Addition and subtraction associate to the {{c1::left}}; exponentiation associates to the {{c2::right}}

cards.front:
What does this print?
print(2 + 3 * 4)
cards.back: 14 — multiplication has higher precedence than addition

cards.front:
What does this print?
print(2 ** 3 ** 2)
cards.back: 512 — ** associates right, so it is 2 ** (3 ** 2), not (2 ** 3) ** 2

cards.front:
What does this print?
print(10 - 3 - 2)
cards.back: 5 — subtraction associates left, so (10 - 3) - 2

cards.front: What is the recommended practice for operator order?
cards.back: Use parentheses to be completely clear

cards.front: What does == test?
cards.back: Whether values are equivalent in meaning — not memory location or anything else

cards.front: What does != test?
cards.back: Whether two values are not equivalent

cards.front: Which four ordering comparisons does Python provide?
cards.back: <, <=, >, >=

cards.front: What does chaining comparisons amount to?
cards.back: Asking two questions at once, both of which must be true

cards.front:
What does this print?
x = 3
print(0 < x < 5)
cards.back: True — the chain is both 0 < x and x < 5

cards.text: Boolean operators: negate with {{c1::not}}, combine with {{c2::and}} or {{c3::or}}

cards.front: What does Python require you to declare about a variable's type?
cards.back: Nothing — Python is implicitly typed, so you never declare a type

cards.front: What does it take to create a variable in Python?
cards.back: Assign a value to it — boo = 11

cards.front:
What does this print?
boo = 11
print(boo)
cards.back: 11 — the name evaluates to the value assigned

cards.front: What makes boo = 11 a statement rather than an expression?
cards.back: It gives back no value — it works by side effect

cards.text: An {{c1::expression}} gives back a value; a {{c2::statement}} gives back nothing and works by {{c3::side effect}}

cards.front: What low-level work does Python spare you when using variables?
cards.back: Declaring a type, requesting memory, and worrying about stack versus heap

cards.front: In Python, what carries a type — the variable or the value?
cards.back: The value. Variables have no type at all, which is why one can later hold a different type

cards.front: Can a variable hold a different type later on?
cards.back: Yes, though it is not best practice

cards.front: What is Python's naming convention for variables?
cards.back: snake_case — lowercase words joined by underscores

cards.front: What naming convention do Python script files use?
cards.back: The same as variables — snake_case

cards.front: How do you run a script normally from the command line?
cards.back: python3 filename.py

cards.front: How do you run a script and stay in the shell afterwards?
cards.back:
python3 -i -m filename
The module name, without the .py

cards.text: {{c1::python3 filename.py}} runs the script and exits; {{c2::python3 -i -m filename}} runs it and leaves you in the shell

cards.front: How can a program evaluate an expression the way the shell does?
cards.back: With the built-in eval()

cards.front: What is the danger of eval()?
cards.back: It has serious pitfalls — above all code injection: it will execute whatever string it is handed

cards.front: How many arguments can print take, and how are they separated by default?
cards.back: As many as you like — separated by spaces

cards.front: What decides how an object appears when passed to print?
cards.back: The object itself — every object defines its own behaviour for being printed

cards.front: Which keyword argument of print controls what goes between the arguments?
cards.back: sep

cards.front: Which keyword argument of print controls what goes after everything?
cards.back: end

cards.text: print's {{c1::sep}} sets what falls between the arguments; {{c2::end}} sets what follows the last one

cards.front: What kind of argument are sep and end, and how common are they?
cards.back: Keyword arguments — something only some functions allow

cards.front:
What does this print?
print(1, 2, 3)
cards.back: 1 2 3 — spaces by default

cards.front:
What does this print?
print(1, 2, 3, sep='+')
cards.back: 1+2+3

cards.front:
What does this print?
print('a', end='-')
print('b')
cards.back: a-b — end replaces the usual newline

cards.front: Which built-in function reads input?
cards.back: input()

cards.front: What must you do to keep what input() gives back?
cards.back: Store it in a variable — it returns a value, and an uncaught value is lost

cards.front: What type does input() always return?
cards.back: A string

cards.front: What is the type name for a string?
cards.back: str

cards.front: What is a string?
cards.back: A sequence of characters

cards.front: How do you write a string literal?
cards.back: Enclose it in single or double quotes

cards.front: Which quotes does this class prefer?
cards.back: Single quotes

cards.front: What counts as a “character” in Python?
cards.back: A string with one character in it — there is no separate character type

cards.front: What practical use comes from having both quote styles?
cards.back: You can put quotes inside a string literal by enclosing it in the other kind

cards.front: What is the other way to put special characters in a string?
cards.back: Escape sequences, using a backslash

cards.front: What does len() give you for a string?
cards.back: Its length

cards.front: Does len() measure the string or the literal that produced it?
cards.back: The string itself — the two are not necessarily equal

cards.front: Do all objects have a length?
cards.back: No

cards.text: Strings support {{c1::+}} to concatenate and {{c2::*}} to repeat; {{c3::subtraction and division}} have no meaning for them

cards.front: What does == compare for strings?
cards.back: Their value — not memory or anything else

cards.front: What does .strip() do to the string you call it on?
cards.back: Nothing — it returns a new string with the whitespace removed, leaving the original untouched

cards.front: Which other string methods behave the same way as .strip()?
cards.back: .upper() — it also returns a new string rather than changing the original

cards.front: What does .isupper() return?
cards.back: A bool

cards.front: On what can string methods be called, besides variables?
cards.back: Literals — you can call a method directly on 'hello'

cards.front:
What does this print?
print('ab' * 3)
cards.back: ababab

cards.front:
What does this print?
s = '  hi  '
s.strip()
print(s)
cards.back: ' hi ' with its spaces intact — .strip() returns a new string and never changes the original

cards.front:
What does this print?
print(len('a\tb'))
cards.back: 3 — the escape sequence is one character, though the literal is four

cards.front: What is a range?
cards.back: A sequence of numbers

cards.front: How many arguments does the range() constructor take?
cards.back: Up to three

cards.text: range()'s arguments: {{c1::start — inclusive}}, {{c2::stop — exclusive}}, {{c3::step — the distance between numbers, optional and 1 by default}}

cards.front: Which end of a range is included and which is not?
cards.back: The start is included; the stop is excluded

cards.front: How do you get at an individual number in a range?
cards.back: Index into it with []

cards.front: What does the single argument mean in range(5)?
cards.back: The stop, not the start — it gives 0 through 4. Not stated in the lecture, which describes the three-argument form.

cards.front: What is a method, in terms of what you are doing?
cards.back: Asking an object to perform something on your behalf

cards.front: On what are methods called?
cards.back: Objects

cards.front: What does method chaining look like, and why does it work?
cards.back: description.upper().isupper() — each call returns an object that the next method is then called on

cards.front: How do you convert between types?
cards.back: Call the type like a function — int('35'). This is an object constructor

cards.front: What does bool give for a string?
cards.back: True for a non-empty string, False for an empty one

cards.front: How does Python mark a block?
cards.back: By indentation

cards.front: What is the standard indentation width?
cards.back: Four spaces

cards.front: What is the syntax of an if statement, and what is the convention about parentheses?
cards.back: if expression: — the norm is no parentheses around the expression

cards.front: Must the expression in an if statement evaluate to a bool?
cards.back: No — it undergoes a truth test instead

cards.front: How much of Python falls into “truthy” or “falsy”?
cards.back: Everything — every object is one or the other

cards.text: Truth tests: an empty string is {{c1::falsy}} and a non-empty one {{c2::truthy}}; the number {{c3::0}} is falsy and every other number truthy

cards.front:
What does this print?
if '0':
    print('yes')
if 0:
    print('no')
cards.back: yes only — '0' is a non-empty string so it is truthy, while the number 0 is falsy

cards.front: What is the syntax of a while loop, and what rules govern its expression?
cards.back: while expression: — the same expression rules as an if statement

cards.front: Which loop form does Python lack?
cards.back: do-while

cards.front: What can a while loop carry that is unusual, and when does it run?
cards.back: An else clause — it runs when the test fails

cards.front: What stops a while loop's else clause from running?
cards.back: Leaving the loop through break — the else runs only when the test fails. Not stated in the lecture.

cards.front: What does break do?
cards.back: Leaves the loop immediately

cards.meaning: an assignment that is also an expression — it returns the value assigned

cards.front: What makes the walrus operator different from an ordinary assignment?
cards.back: An ordinary assignment is a statement and gives nothing back; the walrus is an expression and returns the value assigned

cards.front:
What does this print?
if (n := 5) > 3:
    print(n)
cards.back: 5 — the walrus assigns and returns in one step, so n is usable straight away

cards.front: Why break a problem into functions that know as little about each other as possible?
cards.back: To avoid the “avalanche of complexity” — each small piece stays understandable on its own

cards.front: Which keyword defines a function?
cards.back: def

cards.front: What is the difference between an argument and a parameter?
cards.back: An argument is what you pass into a function; it lands inside the function as a parameter

cards.front: What happens when a return statement is reached?
cards.back: Its expression is evaluated, and control goes back to whatever called the function, carrying that value

cards.front: What does a function give back if it never reaches a return?
cards.back: None — a function always returns a value

cards.front:
What does this print?
def f():
    return 1

print(f)
cards.back: Something like <function f at 0x…> — naming a function without parentheses is legal; it gives the function object and its memory address, without calling it

cards.front: Which argument types will Python accept for a function's parameters?
cards.back: Any — as long as what the function does with them is legal

cards.front: What is a docstring?
cards.back: A string literal as the first line of a function, describing what it does

cards.front: What does a long, complicated docstring suggest?
cards.back: That the function is doing too much

cards.text: A docstring longer than one line uses {{c1::''', a multi-line string literal}}; you read a docstring back with {{c2::function_name.__doc__}}

cards.front: When must a function be defined, relative to its use?
cards.back: Before it is called

cards.front: When a name exists both globally and locally, which one does Python use?
cards.back: The most local one

cards.text: Python looks a name up in this order: {{c1::local}}, {{c2::enclosing}}, {{c3::global}}, {{c4::built-in}}

cards.front: What is the enclosing scope?
cards.back: With nested functions: the local scope of the function in which the inner function is defined

cards.front: Which variables are local to a function call?
cards.back: Every variable assigned inside it, its parameters included — local to that one call

cards.front:
What does this print?
q = 1

def f():
    print(q)
    q = 2

f()
cards.back: Nothing — it raises UnboundLocalError. Python parses the whole function first, sees q assigned, and treats it as local throughout; at the print it exists but has no value yet.

cards.front:
What does this print?
name = 'Boo'
print(f'Hi {name}')
cards.back: Hi Boo — an f before a string literal lets you put values into it in braces

cards.front: What is a tuple?
cards.back: An immutable sequence of values, of any mixture of types

cards.front: What does it mean that a tuple is immutable, and what else behaves that way?
cards.back: You can't change it — you build a new one instead, just as with a string

cards.front: What does it mean that a tuple is a sequence?
cards.back: The order of its values matters

cards.front: When is a tuple the natural choice?
cards.back: When, before the program runs, you know how many values you need and what each one is

cards.front: How do you write a tuple literal, and when do you need the parentheses?
cards.back: Expressions separated by commas: ('Boo', 11, 3.5). Parentheses are needed where it would otherwise be ambiguous — in a function call, where commas separate arguments.

cards.front: Which operations does a tuple share with a string?
cards.back: Taking its length with len(), and indexing with []

cards.front:
What does this print?
point = 34, 28
x, y = point
print(y)
cards.back: 28 — sequence assignment unpacks anything iterable into a matching sequence of variables

cards.front: How do you swap two variables in one line?
cards.back: a, b = b, a

cards.front: What is a list, and how is it written differently from a tuple?
cards.back: A mutable sequence of objects, written in square brackets: [1, 2, 3]

cards.front:
What does this print?
x = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
print(x[-1])
cards.back: 5 — a negative index counts from the end: [0] is the first element, [-1] the last

cards.front: What does .append() do to a list?
cards.back: Adds one element to the end — changing the list itself

cards.front:
What does this print?
x = [1, 2]
x.append([3, 4])
print(x)
cards.back: [1, 2, [3, 4]] — appending a list nests it as a single element, since an element can be of any type

cards.front: How do you add another list's elements to a list, rather than nesting the list?
cards.back: .extend(), or += — a concatenation, as with strings

cards.front: How do you replace one element of a list, and how do you delete one?
cards.back: Assign by index, x[3] = 5; delete with del x[5]

cards.front: What does calling list() on an iterable do?
cards.back: Builds a new list from its values

cards.front:
What does this print?
x = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]
print(x[3:7])
cards.back: [3, 4, 5, 6] — like a range, a slice's start is inclusive and its stop exclusive

cards.text: In a slice, leaving out the start means {{c1::from index 0}}; leaving out the stop means {{c2::to the end of the list}}; the optional third value is {{c3::the step, as in a range}}
cards.extra: Your notes say the stop defaults to -1, but x[3:-1] leaves out the last element. An omitted stop runs to the end.

cards.front:
What does this print?
x = [1, 2, 3]
print(x[::-1])
cards.back: [3, 2, 1] — a negative step walks backwards, so this builds a reversed copy (ranges can step backwards too)

cards.front: What do type annotations do, and what don't they do?
cards.back: They state your intentions about types; Python doesn't enforce them — it's dynamically typed, and types are dealt with as the program runs

cards.front: What can be given a type annotation?
cards.back: Variables, function parameters, function return types, and more

cards.front: If annotations aren't enforced, what makes them useful?
cards.back: Tools such as VS Code flag code that contradicts them

cards.front: From when are type annotations required in ICS H32?
cards.back: From Project 1

cards.front: How do you annotate a parameter and a return type?
cards.back: A colon and the type after the parameter, and -> and the type after the parameter list: def f(x: int) -> str:

cards.front: After an annotation's colon, what can you technically write, and what should you write?
cards.back: Any legal Python expression — but you should write a type, such as str

cards.text: Annotating a value that may be one of several types: {{c1::int | float}}; a tuple: {{c2::tuple[type1, type2]}}; a list: {{c3::list[int], naming its elements' type}}; a list of mixed elements: {{c4::list[int | float]}}

cards.front: What is a file?
cards.back: A container in which a sequence of bytes is stored — the basic abstraction of a file system

cards.front: What is a byte?
cards.back: A sequence of eight bits, each either 1 or 0

cards.front: What do file names mean to the computer?
cards.back: Nothing — they mean something only to humans. A name ending in .jpg is essentially a guess about the contents.

cards.front: What does \n stand for in Python?
cards.back: An abstraction of whatever the system uses to mark a newline — which differs between systems

cards.front: Why clean data the moment it comes into your program?
cards.back: Then you never have to deal with it later, and the rest of the program can focus on its own job

cards.front: What does open() take, and what does it return?
cards.back: A path, absolute or relative, and a mode — 'r' to read or 'w' to write, as text. It returns a file object.

cards.front: What is pathlib's Path for?
cards.back: You pass it a string, and it works out the right path for your system

cards.front: What does the / operator do with a Path?
cards.back: Appends to it — joining on the next part of the path

cards.text: On a Path: {{c1::.exists()}} says whether it's on your machine; {{c2::.is_file() and .is_dir()}} say what kind it is; {{c3::.open()}} opens it as open() does; {{c4::.iterdir()}} gives an iterable over a directory's contents

cards.front: How do you get a directory's contents as a list?
cards.back: Pass the iterable to the list constructor: list(p.iterdir())

cards.front: What does a file object's .mode tell you?
cards.back: Which mode it was opened in — read or write

cards.front: What happens if you open a file that doesn't exist in 'w' mode?
cards.back: It's created

cards.front: Why close a file as soon as you no longer need it?
cards.back: An open file can affect how other programs can access it

cards.front: Why can data you wrote to a file be lost, and what prevents it?
cards.back: Writes go to a buffer in memory, written out only when it fills, so a program that stops early can lose them. .close() saves them; .flush() empties the buffer on demand.

cards.front: What, physically, is a “line” in a text file?
cards.back: Nothing in itself — just characters that tell software to show a line break

cards.front: What does .readline() return, and what does it do to the file's cursor?
cards.back: The text from the cursor up to and including the next newline, if there is one — and it moves the cursor to the next line

cards.front: What does it mean when .readline() returns an empty string?
cards.back: You're at the end of the file — an empty line still gives '\n'

cards.front: What does opening a file in 'w' mode do to it, and what does .write() then do?
cards.back: Opening in 'w' empties the file; each .write() then adds the string you pass it at the cursor

cards.front: What kinds of failure can hit a program that is itself correct?
cards.back: Failures from outside it — a file that can't be opened, bad input

cards.front: What is an exception?
cards.back: An object that represents failure

cards.front: What does a traceback show?
cards.back: Where the problem happened, and how the program got to that line — traced outward through the calls

cards.front: What does a function return when it raises an exception?
cards.back: No value at all

cards.front: What happens to the rest of a try block when a statement in it raises an exception?
cards.back: It's skipped — you leave the try block immediately

cards.text: After try:, except runs {{c1::if an exception is raised}}; else runs {{c2::after the try block, if no exception was raised}}; finally runs {{c3::after the try block, no matter what happened}}

cards.front: How do you narrow an except clause, and why should you?
cards.back: Name the type of exception after it — exceptions fall into categories. Specific clauses can be chained, and being specific is better.

cards.front: How do you raise an exception yourself?
cards.back: raise with a type and a message: raise ValueError('Bad input!')

cards.front: What is a socket?
cards.back: One end of a connection, provided by the operating system — like a tin can on a string, with a socket at the other end

cards.front: What two streams does a socket have?
cards.back: An input stream and an output stream

cards.front: What ordering does the course rely on for messages over a connection?
cards.back: They arrive in the order they were sent, or not at all — even though the pieces may be received out of order

cards.front: Why are networked programs more fallible than local ones?
cards.back: External circumstances can break the connection

cards.front: Of two programs on a connection, which is the client and which the server?
cards.back: The one that establishes the connection is the client, connecting; the one that accepts it is the server, listening

cards.front: What is the loopback address?
cards.back: 127.0.0.1 — your own machine

cards.front: What is a port, and what range do port numbers cover?
cards.back: A number naming one place on a machine where a program might be listening — 0 to 65535, that is 2¹⁶ values. Some ports are standard.

cards.front: How do you create a socket in Python?
cards.back: import socket, then socket.socket()

cards.front: How does a client connect, and how do you know it worked?
cards.back: Call connect((host, port)) with a tuple; it worked if no exception was raised

cards.front: How do you get file-like objects for a socket's two streams?
cards.back: makefile('r') for input and makefile('w') for output — pseudo-file objects

cards.front: How do you send a line through a socket's output file, and why the second step?
cards.back: .write() the string, then .flush() so the buffer is actually sent

cards.front: What does .readline() on a socket's input do to newline sequences?
cards.back: It collapses them back to \n

cards.front: In what order do you close a socket connection?
cards.back: The input, then the output, then the socket

cards.front: How do you know when something you're writing is done, and what's the better way to check?
cards.back: Run it and see if it works — better, automate it: write programs that test your programs

cards.front: What does an assert statement do?
cards.back: States something you believe to be true; if it's false, an exception — AssertionError — is raised

cards.front:
What does this print?
assert 10 > 8, 'making sure the universe still maths'
cards.back: Nothing — the condition is true. If it were false, an AssertionError with that message would be raised.

cards.front: How do you test that code raises the exception you expect?
cards.back:
try:
    remove_all([1, 3, 5, 7, 8], 99)
    assert False, 'ValueError should have been raised'
except ValueError:
    pass
Put an assert False after the call that should fail, and catch the expected exception.

cards.front: What will the course teach later about tests?
cards.back: How to separate tests from the code

cards.front: What is a namedtuple?
cards.back: A tuple in which each element is explicitly given a name

cards.front: How do you get namedtuple objects?
cards.back: First make a blueprint — a new type — with namedtuple; then create objects from that type

cards.front: Where does namedtuple come from?
cards.back: The collections module: from collections import namedtuple

cards.front: What two arguments does namedtuple take?
cards.back: A string naming the new type, and a list of strings naming its fields

cards.front:
What does this print?
from collections import namedtuple
Point = namedtuple('Point', ['x', 'y'])
p = Point(1, 2)
print(p._replace(y=5))
cards.back: Point(x=1, y=5) — ._replace() returns a new object of the same type with the named fields replaced; p itself is unchanged

cards.front:
What does this print?
from collections import namedtuple
Point = namedtuple('Point', ['x', 'y'])
print(Point._fields)
cards.back: ('x', 'y') — ._fields gives the names of the fields

cards.front: What is recursion?
cards.back: A function calling itself in its own definition — something you can't do when defining a word

cards.front: What should you try before reaching for recursion?
cards.back: A loop

cards.front: What is a set's defining characteristic?
cards.back: Order makes no difference — the only thing that matters is membership

cards.front: How do you write a set literal?
cards.back: Expressions in curly braces, separated by commas: {1, 2, 3}

cards.front: How do you write an empty set, and why not {}?
cards.back: set() — {} on its own is an empty dictionary

cards.front: How do you test whether something is in a set, and why use a set for it?
cards.back: With in. It works on lists too, but sets are optimised for exactly this.

cards.text: Set operators: {{c1::|}} gives the union; {{c2::&}} the intersection; {{c3::-}} the difference; {{c4::^}} the symmetric difference

cards.front:
What does this print?
print({1, 2} | {2, 3})
cards.back: {1, 2, 3} — the union; 2 appears once, since a set holds each value only once

cards.front: Why can't you index into a set, and what can you do instead?
cards.back: It has no fixed order — but you can iterate over it

cards.front: How do you change a set's contents?
cards.back: With .add() and .remove() — sets are mutable

cards.front: What does a dictionary do?
cards.back: Maps keys to values — essentially a keyed set, and also written with curly braces

cards.front: How do you write a dict literal?
How do you read, assign and delete a dictionary entry?
cards.back: Index it by key — d['a'] and d['a'] = 5 — and delete with del d['a']
a, then b — iterating a dictionary gives its keys

cards.front: How do you iterate over a dictionary's values, and over its key–value pairs?
cards.back: .values() for the values; .items() for the pairs, each a tuple
